solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Andrew associated with British spirit

parts.note: Andy is the usual short form of the name Andrew

explanation.surface: A man called Andrew is linked with some British drink or with the national character.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end; the pieces go in answer order with British first, though Andrew comes first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandy is a distilled liquor, and spirit is the general word for such strong alcoholic drinks.

clue.text: Barbara rings Yankee — it's to mind infant

indicators.note: rings means encircles, so the name's short form goes round the letter for Yankee

parts.note: Babs is a familiar short form of Barbara
Y is Yankee in the NATO phonetic alphabet
it gives IT, with the 's read as a joining 'is'

explanation.surface: Barbara phones an American, saying it is her turn to look after the baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rings' looks like telephoning but means surrounding: BABS goes round Y.
explanation.definitionFit: To babysit is to look after a young child while the parents are out.

clue.text: Hate having a house in Bangor's outskirts

indicators.note: in places the house abbreviation within the two edge letters
outskirts are the edges of a town, so only the first and last letters of the place name are kept

explanation.surface: Someone loathes owning a home on the edge of the Welsh city of Bangor.
explanation.walkthrough: Bangor is a city in north Wales; its outskirts are B and R, with HO set between them after A.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to detest it, so the verb is a close synonym of hate.

clue.text: Fiend started to stir and protested publicly

parts.note: a fiend is a demon

indicators.note: to stir is to mix things up, so the letters of the next word are jumbled

explanation.surface: A villain began causing trouble and people took to the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' fits the picture of agitators, but 'to stir' is the anagram signal working on the word started.
explanation.definitionFit: To demonstrate is to take part in a public protest or march.

clue.text: Catch sight of small earthenware vessel

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a pot is a vessel, often made of earthenware

explanation.surface: Notice a little clay pot, perhaps at an antiques fair.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot something is to notice or glimpse it, a direct synonym of catching sight.

clue.text: Writer and Italian poet mostly hanging ornament

parts.note: a pen is something you write with

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the poet's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Dante Alighieri is the great Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: An author and an Italian poet are mentioned together with a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' looks like a person but is the instrument, PEN; 'mostly' trims DANTE to DANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A pendant is jewellery that hangs from a chain round the neck.

clue.text: English river split after junction

indicators.note: after puts the word for split behind the letter for junction

parts.note: a T-junction is where one road meets another, so T stands for junction
a rent is a split or tear

explanation.surface: A river divides just beyond the point where it meets another.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trent flows through the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trent is one of England's major rivers, flowing through the Midlands to the Humber.

clue.text: Beware! Large hole underground

definitions.meaning: Latin for beware, once shouted by schoolboys as a warning that a teacher was coming
a large hollow beneath the ground or in a hillside

explanation.surface: A warning shout about a big pit hidden below the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin warning cave is pronounced 'kay-vee', unlike the English word, and was old British schoolboy slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin imperative means take care, and the English noun names a natural hollow in rock.

clue.text: GI with clean house rearranged item of furniture

indicators.note: rearranged means put in a different order, so these letters are shuffled together

explanation.surface: An American soldier tidies up the place and moves a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rearranged' shuffles GICLEANHOUSE; GI is a US soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaise longue is a long upholstered couch, a piece of furniture for reclining.

clue.text: Snake around border with India, finding ancient kingdom

indicators.note: around puts the snake's letters on either side of what follows

parts.note: a boa is a large snake
a hem is the edge or border of cloth
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A snake found near the Indian frontier leads to a lost realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps the snake's letters about the border and India pieces; 'finding' only links them to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bohemia was a medieval kingdom in central Europe, now the western part of the Czech Republic.

clue.text: Some heathen celebrated from this time

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some pagans have held a festival ever since a particular moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Hence in its older sense means from now on, as in 'two years hence'.

clue.text: African National Park's remarkably green site

indicators.note: remarkably suggests something out of the ordinary, so the letters take an unusual order

explanation.surface: A famous African reserve is described as a strikingly lush place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remarkably' turns GREENSITE into the answer; the 's after Park reads as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti in Tanzania is one of Africa's best-known wildlife reserves.

clue.text: Fitting carpet regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of carpet is taken

explanation.surface: Laying a carpet at regular intervals, as a fitter might.
explanation.definitionFit: Apt means suitable or appropriate, as does fitting used as an adjective.

clue.text: Fruit also covers rug

indicators.note: covers says the word for also wraps round the floor covering

parts.note: too means also
a mat is a small rug

explanation.surface: Fruit is also used to cover a rug, an odd household scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covers' means the word for also wraps round the rug word, splitting open to hold it rather than lying on top.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the tomato is a fruit, the seed-bearing part of the plant.

clue.text: Drunk embraces copper — it may indicate warmth

indicators.note: embraces means holds within, so the chemical symbol sits inside the word for drunk

parts.note: merry is a mild word for tipsy
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A drunk hugs a policeman, which may show affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but is the element, CU. The definition refers to a thermometer reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercury is the liquid metal in a traditional thermometer, rising to show heat.

clue.text: Held in enclosure: sheep

parts.note: a pen is an enclosure for animals
a tup is a ram, a male sheep

explanation.surface: A sheep is kept inside a fold.
explanation.walkthrough: TUP is a dialect word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Pent-up means confined or restrained, as feelings held in are.

clue.text: Perhaps Band Aid record brought back tears when broadcast

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the record abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: The charity record Band Aid made people cry when it was played on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns LP into PL; 'broadcast' rearranges TEARS into ASTER. Band Aid is a brand of sticking plaster as well as the 1984 charity group.
explanation.definitionFit: A Band-Aid is a brand of adhesive dressing, which British English calls a plaster; 'Perhaps' marks it as an example.

clue.text: Jolt container

explanation.surface: A shock to a storage pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Jar is both a verb for a sudden jarring shock and a noun for a pot with a lid.

clue.text: Lucky having two minutes surrounded by colourful bird

indicators.note: surrounded by puts the minutes inside the bird's name

parts.note: the jay is a brightly coloured member of the crow family
M is the abbreviation for minute, so two minutes gives MM

explanation.surface: Someone is fortunate to get a couple of minutes near a bright bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounded by' puts the two minutes inside the bird's name. Jammy is British slang for lucky.
explanation.definitionFit: Jammy is informal British slang for fortunate, especially undeservedly so.

clue.text: New roadmen returning notice group of stars

indicators.note: new suggests a fresh form, so the letters are rearranged
returning means going back, so the word for notice is read backwards

parts.note: an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: Fresh road workers are coming back to a notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges ROADMEN into ANDROME; 'returning' turns AD into DA.
explanation.definitionFit: Andromeda is a constellation of the northern sky, named after the princess of Greek myth.

clue.text: Five inside exit disreputable place

indicators.note: inside puts the numeral within the word for exit

parts.note: to exit is a euphemism for to die, as in leaving the stage of life
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Five people leave through the exit of a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exit' looks like a doorway but is the verb, die.
explanation.definitionFit: A dive is slang for a shabby, disreputable bar or club.

clue.text: Upright European reportedly ruined

indicators.note: reportedly means as people say, so the following word is taken by its sound

parts.note: ruined means wrecked

explanation.surface: A European is said to have been ruined.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means standing straight up, so it is a synonym of upright.

clue.text: Rodent marks domestic 'abitat?

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for marks, the old German currency
a domestic habitat is a house; the apostrophe in 'abitat signals a dropped H, so it becomes OUSE

explanation.surface: A rodent leaves marks around the home, spoken in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the H, as in Cockney speech, turns HOUSE into OUSE; the clue shows this with 'abitat.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouse is a small rodent, commonly found in houses.

clue.text: V & A visitor most uncertain

parts.note: the letters of the V & A, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London
a guest is a visitor

explanation.surface: A visitor to London's Victoria and Albert Museum is very unsure.
explanation.walkthrough: The V & A is the Victoria and Albert Museum, a London museum of art and design.
explanation.definitionFit: Vague means unclear or uncertain, so the superlative means the least certain.

clue.text: Lout repeatedly clipped child's toy

indicators.note: repeatedly says the shortened word is used twice
clipped means cut short, so the word for lout loses its last letter

parts.note: a yob is a lout, a thug

explanation.surface: A hooligan keeps hitting a child's plaything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clipped' trims YOB to YO, and 'repeatedly' doubles it. Yob is British slang for a lout.
explanation.definitionFit: A yo-yo is a spool on a string that a child spins up and down.

clue.text: Briefly drink black stuff, a delicious beverage

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word for drink loses its last letter

parts.note: to neck is British slang for to drink quickly
tar is a black sticky substance

explanation.surface: Quickly downing a dark drink, perhaps stout, which tastes wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' trims NECK to NEC. To neck a drink is British slang for gulping it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nectar was the drink of the gods in Greek myth, so it names any delicious drink.
